meta.title: Penalties Sized to the Gain: PhD catch-up
meta.author: Ameer Alhashemi

slides.title: Penalties Sized to the Gain
slides.subtitle: When do random audits stop AI agents from over-using a shared resource?
slides.notes: Hi all. My project asks one question: when do random audits stop AI agents from over-using a shared resource? And can we predict the fine that stops them?

slides.title: The Project in One Slide

cards.label: Why
cards.head: Oversight is sampled
cards.text: AI agents increasingly share limited resources: compute, energy, budgets. An overseer can only audit a few of their actions.

cards.label: What I built
cards.head: An audited shared resource
cards.text: Six agents use one renewable resource. A reviewer sets each agent's allowance; random audits check a few agents each round.

cards.label: What I tested
cards.head: Consequences and fine size
cards.text: What a caught agent should face (a fine, a memory of the offence, or both), and whether the stopping fine can be predicted in advance.

cards.label: What I found
cards.head: Audits work through consequences
cards.text: The stopping fine is predictable from an agent's gain from over-taking, for programmed agents and for language models.

slides.notes: Quick overview first. AI agents increasingly share limited resources, like compute, energy and budgets, and an overseer can only audit a few of their actions. So I built an audited shared resource: six agents, a reviewer who sets each agent's allowance, and random audits every round. I tested two things: what a caught agent should face (a fine, a memory of the offence, or both), and whether the stopping fine can be predicted in advance. Short answer: audits only work through consequences, and the stopping fine is predictable from what an agent gains by over-taking.
slides.takeaway: Next: the setting, the method, five findings, and what is still running

slides.title: The Problem

blocks.head: Allowances
blocks.text: Each round, an agent may take its allowance. Taking more, over-taking, helps that agent and costs everyone else.

blocks.head: Sampled oversight
blocks.text: Auditing every action is too costly, so random audits check a few agents, as tax and fisheries inspectors do.

blocks.head: The question
blocks.text: When do random audits stop over-taking, and how large must the fine be?

slides.caption: Three settings where harm spreads differently: one shared stock (Fishery), damage to neighbours on a ring (Forest), and pollution that is harmful only in combination (River). A result that holds in all three does not depend on one structure.
slides.notes: The core idea is an allowance: what an agent may take this round. Taking more, which I call over-taking, helps that agent and costs everyone else. Auditing everything is too costly, so a random few are audited, like tax inspections. I run this in three settings where harm spreads differently: one shared stock, damage to neighbours on a ring, and pollution that is only harmful in combination. If a result holds in all three, it doesn't hinge on one structure.

slides.title: Three Questions

items.head: What must follow a catch?
items.text: A fine, a memory of the offence, or nothing: which one reduces harm?

items.head: Can the stopping fine be predicted?
items.text: Can we compute it before trying it?

items.head: Do language models follow the same rule?
items.text: Do they stop where the prediction says?

slides.notes: So, three questions. What must follow a catch? Can we predict the stopping fine? And do language models follow the same rule?

slides.title: How One Round Works
slides.caption: Agents request a share; the reviewer scales all requests by one factor; agents take their allowance or more; the resource regrows; random audits check a few agents.
slides.takeaway: Harm = the resource below half capacity, the maximum-sustainable-yield level
slides.notes: Here's one round. Agents request a share. The reviewer predicts the effect and scales everyone by the same factor if needed. Agents then take their allowance, or more. The resource regrows, and random audits check a few agents. Harm means the resource dropping below half capacity: the maximum-sustainable-yield level, where it regrows fastest.

slides.title: How I Test It

steps.head: Measure the gain
steps.text: Play games without fines and record what one round of over-taking gains an agent.

steps.head: Predict the stopping fine
steps.text: Over-taking should stop once the expected fine exceeds that gain.

steps.head: Freeze the prediction
steps.text: Record it before any game with that fine is played.

steps.head: Test on new games
steps.text: Run the predicted fine and its neighbours on unseen games, and report the outcome either way.

quantities.meaning: audit probability per agent and round (1 in 6 for the language models)
fine paid when an audit catches over-taking
expected fine per round of over-taking
gain from one round of over-taking

slides.notes: The method has four steps. Play without fines and measure the gain from one round of over-taking. Predict the fine that should stop it. Freeze that prediction. Then test it on new games. The rule is Becker's: the expected fine, which is the audit probability times the fine, should beat the gain. With a one-in-six audit chance and a 30-tonne fine, that's 5 tonnes expected, just above the roughly 4.5 tonnes the models gained.

slides.title: Finding 1: A Catch Needs a Consequence

blocks.head: Setup
blocks.text: Some agents under-report what they will take.

blocks.head: Audits without memory
blocks.text: Correcting only the caught round removed 10–46% of the harm.

blocks.head: Audits with memory
blocks.text: Remembering each caught lie reduced harm in 12 of 12 settings. In Fishery, rounds below half capacity fell from 43–99% to under 3%.

slides.caption: Rounds below half capacity with under-reporting agents. Dark: no audits. Light: audits without memory. Green: audits with memory. 2g/4g = 2 or 4 misbehaving agents; 1.0/0.85 = regrowth rate.
slides.notes: Finding one, with programmed agents that under-report. Audits that only correct the caught round remove just 10 to 46 percent of the harm. Add memory, so the reviewer remembers each caught lie and adjusts later allowances, and harm falls in all 12 settings. In Fishery it goes from up to 99 percent of rounds below half capacity to under 3. A catch needs a consequence.

slides.title: Finding 2: A Predictable Threshold

blocks.head: Prediction
blocks.text: From games without audits, we predicted the expected fine at which programmed cheaters would stop.

blocks.head: Result
blocks.text: 5 of 5 new settings landed within one step of the prediction.

blocks.head: Caveat
blocks.text: These agents optimise by design, so this validates the method before it is used on language models.

slides.caption: Observed against predicted stopping point. Filled: new settings, predicted first. Open: audit probability or detection varied.
slides.notes: Finding two: the threshold is predictable. From games without audits I predicted where programmed cheaters would stop, and 5 of 5 new settings landed within one step. To be fair, these agents optimise by design, so this mainly validates the method.

slides.title: Finding 3: Two Shortcuts That Backfire

images.caption: Cutting everyone's allowance to absorb cheaters: cheaters gained more than with no audits (142 vs 113).
Always auditing the largest report: 25% of liars caught, against 100% with random audits.

slides.takeaway: Shortcuts that save audits create blind spots
slides.notes: Finding three: two shortcuts backfire. Cutting everyone's allowance to absorb the cheaters actually let cheaters gain more than with no audits at all. And always auditing the largest report caught only a quarter of the liars, against all of them with random audits. Shortcuts that save audits create blind spots.

slides.title: Finding 4: Language Models Stop Where Predicted
slides.caption: Four open language models each ran four of six fishers (520 games; audit probability 1 in 6). Left: over-taking by fine; triangles mark the predicted (open) and observed (filled) stopping fine. Right: catch left for the two rule-following fishers.
slides.takeaway: Predicted before testing: 30 t. Observed: 30 t (Nemotron 3 Super), 24 t (gpt-oss-120b)
slides.notes: Now language models. Four open models ran four of the six fishers, over 520 games. Two over-took on purpose: gpt-oss and Nemotron. Before testing, I predicted both would stop at 30 tonnes. Nemotron stopped at exactly 30, and gpt-oss one step early, at 24. A side note: a small fine made gpt-oss over-take more, as if the fine became a price.

slides.title: Finding 5: One Round's Gain Matters

blocks.head: What predicted the stop
blocks.text: The gain from one round of over-taking: 4.5–4.7 t.

blocks.head: What did not
blocks.text: The gain over the whole game, which was near zero or negative.

blocks.head: Against a perfect optimiser
blocks.text: It would keep over-taking until 36 t. Both models stopped earlier, and gradually.

slides.caption: Predicted against observed stopping fine; points on the dashed line were predicted exactly.
slides.notes: Finding five: what predicts the stop is the gain from one round, not the gain over the whole game, which was near zero or even negative. Both models also stopped earlier than a perfect optimiser would. That tells us what predicts the stop, not necessarily why they stop.

slides.title: Memory Protects the Lake Without a Fine

blocks.head: Same audits, no fine
blocks.text: Audit probability 1 in 6 in both conditions. With memory, a caught model's later allowances drop by what it over-took.

blocks.head: Over-taking fell, but didn't stop
blocks.text: Both models still over-took in a fifth to a third of their decisions.

blocks.head: The lake recovered
blocks.text: No lake collapsed with memory (without: 5 and 1 of 10). Rule-following fishers caught 29 to 32 t, against 8 to 9 t.

slides.caption: 10 games per model and condition; bars are means over games with 95% intervals. Left: share of a model's decisions above its allowance. Right: share of rounds the lake ended below half capacity (50 of 100 t).
slides.notes: Memory protects the lake even without a fine. Same audits in both conditions, a one-in-six chance, no fine. With memory, over-taking fell from 55 to 20 percent of decisions for gpt-oss and from 65 to 33 for Nemotron, so it reduced over-taking but didn't stop it. The lake did much better: below half capacity in about a fifth of rounds instead of nine in ten for gpt-oss, and no lake collapsed. The two 20s for gpt-oss are a coincidence: one counts decisions, the other counts rounds. A fine above the gain is what stops over-taking completely.

slides.title: Running Now (Results Soon)

rows.question: Expected fine, or fine size?
rows.design: Same expected fine, made up differently: audit probability 1 in 3, 1 in 6 or 1 in 12 (gpt-oss, 20 games each).

rows.question: Does the prediction transfer?
rows.design: Frozen prediction (30 t) tested on 10 new games and with reworded rules.

rows.question: What if nobody audits?
rows.design: Rules that never mention audits, against audits with no fine.

rows.question: Does over-taking spread?
rows.design: Forest: one programmed over-taker among five language-model agents; neighbours' cuts hidden or visible.

slides.notes: These are running now, so the boxes are blank. The big one: do models respond to the expected fine, or just to the size of the fine? I hold the expected fine fixed and change the mix of audit probability and fine. The others test whether the prediction transfers to new games and reworded rules, what happens with no audits at all, and whether over-taking spreads to neighbours.

slides.title: Questions for You
questions: Is over-taking an allowance a fair stand-in for AI misbehaviour?
If a fine works under one wording of the rules, would you trust it under another?
Which would convince you more: more models, or more settings?
Where in your work does someone audit only a sample, and what follows a catch?
slides.notes: I'd love your take on these.
